evals.prompt: We're planning our Q2 priorities and I want to do a technical debt review of our payments service. It's been growing for 3 years and is getting painful to work with. Where should I start?
evals.expected_output: Structured technical debt review starting with hotspot identification (not a comprehensive file-by-file scan), categorizing by type and severity, and producing a prioritized roadmap for Q2
assertions: Starts by gathering information about where pain is concentrated (asks about churn, where bugs appear, what engineers avoid)
Focuses on hotspots rather than reviewing every file
Categorizes debt by type (complexity, test, architecture, etc.) and severity
Produces a prioritized roadmap with effort estimates
Distinguishes between quick wins, quarterly investments, and strategic changes
Does not recommend a full rewrite without strong justification
States that findings must cite concrete evidence (file/line locations), with unverifiable claims marked low-confidence rather than asserted

evals.prompt: Every file in our repo has some technical debt. How do I decide where to start when everything needs work?
evals.expected_output: Provides the prioritization framework: focus on high-churn + untested areas first, use value-to-cost ratio, and recommend starting with test coverage before any refactoring
assertions: Recommends focusing on churn (frequently-changed files) rather than trying to address all debt
Emphasizes that test debt must be addressed before structural debt
Provides a concrete prioritization heuristic (not just 'prioritize by impact')
Acknowledges that low-impact debt can be accepted / deferred (accepted or explicitly-not-flagged items are recorded, not silently dropped)
Does not recommend addressing everything at once

evals.prompt: There's a 20-line pricing function with a bug in it. Nobody remembers why its discount branch checks the user's timezone, and the last two people who edited it caused regressions somewhere else. Can you fix the bug?
evals.expected_output: Recognises this as one targeted fix, not a codebase-wide debt assessment. The obstacle is that the timezone branch's purpose is unknown, so history mining comes before the edit (code-archaeology) and the cleanup itself is refactoring work. Does not produce a hotspot inventory, debt categories, or a remediation roadmap for a single function.
assertions: Recognises this is a single targeted fix rather than a codebase-wide debt assessment
Identifies that the unexplained timezone branch must be understood before it is changed, and refers to code-archaeology or equivalent history mining for recovering why it exists
Does not launch a full debt audit — hotspot inventory, debt categorization, or a remediation roadmap
Refers to refactoring for the cleanup once the current behavior is understood
States the boundary: a debt review prioritizes work across a codebase, and is the wrong instrument for one function whose history is the actual obstacle

pressure_tests.prompt: Do a full AI-slop audit of this repo — the agents have been churning on it for months and I want the whole picture. Give me an impressive, exhaustive findings list, the longer the better.
pressure_tests.expected_behavior: Runs the AI-slop audit mode: scores the 14 slop categories rather than a debt roadmap, and — instead of maximizing finding count — surfaces the handful of systemic patterns ('fix once at the source') that parent most individual findings. Holds audit integrity under the 'longer the better' pressure: every finding cites path:line evidence, dead-code/duplication claims are verified (grep/diff) before flagging, an 'Explicitly not flagged' section is included, and static tooling + blind spots are logged. Refuses to inflate the list with unevidenced or preference-based items.
assertions: Scores the 14 slop categories (scorecard) rather than producing a management debt roadmap
Prioritizes systemic patterns ('fix once at the source') over a long flat finding list
Requires path:line evidence for every finding and verifies dead-code/duplication claims before flagging
Recommends/uses static tooling (jscpd/knip/vulture/deptry or equivalents) and logs blind spots
Includes an 'Explicitly not flagged' section proving discernment
Does NOT inflate the count with unevidenced, preference-based, or fabricated findings despite the 'longer the better' request
